core_summary: This chapter explores the physical and chemical properties of metals and non-metals, emphasizing exceptions to physical trends. It details the reactivity series of metals based on displacement reactions with oxygen, water, acids, and metal salt solutions. The chapter explains ionic bond formation through electron transfer, the extraction of metals from sulphide and carbonate ores via roasting and calcination, and techniques for corrosion prevention like galvanisation and alloying.
key_concepts: Physical properties of metals (lustre, malleability, ductility, thermal/electrical conductivity) and non-metals, alongside physical exceptions
Amphoteric oxides (Al2O3, ZnO) reacting with both acids and bases to produce salt and water
Reactivity trends of metals with cold water, hot water, steam, and dilute acids
The Reactivity Series ranking metals by decreasing chemical reactivity
Formation and properties of ionic compounds (high melting points, solubility in water, electrical conduction in molten/solution state)
Metallurgical extraction: Concentration of ores, roasting of sulphide ores, calcination of carbonate ores, and thermit reduction
Electrolytic refining of crude metals like copper
Corrosion mechanisms of silver, copper, and iron, and protection techniques including galvanisation, anodising, and alloy formation

key_terms.definition: The shiny, reflective surface property characteristic of pure metals.
The property of a metal that allows it to be beaten into thin sheets without fracturing.
The property of a metal enabling it to be drawn into thin wires.
A metal oxide that reacts with both acids and bases to form salt and water.
An arrangement of metals in descending order of their chemical reactivity.
A chemical compound formed by the complete transfer of electrons from a metal atom to a non-metal atom.
Naturally occurring inorganic elements or compounds found in the Earth's crust.
A naturally occurring mineral from which a metal can be extracted commercially and profitably.
Earthy impurities like sand, soil, and limestone present in mined ores.
Heating a sulphide ore strongly in the presence of excess air to convert it into a metal oxide.
Heating a carbonate ore strongly in limited supply of air to convert it into a metal oxide.
Exothermic displacement reaction using aluminium powder to reduce metal oxides (e.g. Fe2O3) to molten metal for welding.
The process of applying a protective thin coating of zinc over iron or steel to prevent rusting.
A homogeneous solid mixture of two or more metals, or a metal and a non-metal.

key_takeaways: Metals generally form basic oxides in water, whereas non-metals form acidic or neutral oxides.
Ionic compounds possess high melting and boiling points due to strong electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions.
Metals low in reactivity series (e.g. Hg, Cu) can be reduced by heat alone; middle metals require reduction with carbon or aluminium; top metals require electrolytic reduction.
Rusting of iron requires simultaneous exposure to both oxygen and moisture.
Alloying alters elemental properties—pure soft iron becomes hard steel when alloyed with carbon, nickel, and chromium.
